text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for type 2 diabetes focuses on lowering and stabilizing blood sugar levels through a combination of lifestyle changes, medications, and regular monitoring.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle changes, medications, and regular monitoring

list.snippet: Healthy Eating: Focus on non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, complex carbohydrates, and heart-healthy fats (such as the Mediterranean or DASH diets).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular exercise to improve insulin sensitivity and lower blood glucose.

Weight Management: Losing even 5% of body weight can significantly improve how the body regulates blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Weight loss surgery (bariatric surgery) is also an option for individuals with obesity.
Blood Sugar Monitoring: Track glucose levels at home using a standard blood glucose meter or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM).

text_blocks.snippet: When diet and exercise are not enough, healthcare providers prescribe oral or injectable medications. Detailed guides and medication classes can be reviewed via the American Diabetes Association:

list.snippet: Metformin (Biguanides): The standard first-line oral medication. It decreases glucose production in the liver and makes muscle and fat cells more sensitive to insulin.
Sulfonylureas: (e.g., glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide) Stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists & GLP-1/GIP Agonists: Injectable medications that boost insulin release, slow digestion, suppress glucagon, and often support weight loss and heart/kidney health.
SGLT2 Inhibitors: Oral medications that help the kidneys remove excess glucose through urine while offering heart and kidney benefits.
DPP-4 Inhibitors (Gliptins): Oral medications that enhance incretin hormones to help lower post-meal blood sugar without causing weight gain.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) Improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat tissue.
Insulin Therapy: Long-acting, short-acting, or rapid-acting insulin injections or pumps may be introduced if oral and injectable medications no longer control blood sugar adequately.
